clue.text: Rousing songs?

parts.note: read as songs that rouse sleepers: the birds singing together at first light, waking everyone

explanation.definitionFit: The birdsong heard at daybreak is what wakes, or rouses, people, so it is literally a set of rousing songs.

clue.text: Plaintiff taking in good old magistrate

indicators.note: the plaintiff is said to take in, or enclose, the next piece, so one goes inside the other

parts.note: John Doe is the traditional fictitious name for a plaintiff in English law

explanation.surface: A litigant bringing an old magistrate into the case on his side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking in' puts G inside DOE. John Doe was the name used for an unnamed plaintiff in old English legal actions.
explanation.definitionFit: The doge was the elected chief ruler and judge of the old republics of Venice and Genoa.

clue.text: Seducer, most deceitful when looking sheepish?

definitions.meaning: a man who persistently chases women is called by this animal's name
the predator in sheep's clothing of the proverb is at its most treacherous when disguised as a sheep

explanation.surface: A womaniser who is at his slyest when he looks embarrassed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sheepish' seems to mean embarrassed, but it means literally dressed as a sheep, as in the proverbial disguised predator.
explanation.definitionFit: A predatory womaniser is slang for this animal, and the fable's disguised beast is most treacherous in a fleece.

clue.text: What well-dressed players put on

parts.note: read 'put on' as staging, not wearing: the kind of period play performed by actors in elaborate dress

explanation.definitionFit: A period play staged with historical dress is something actors in fine clothes perform, 'put on' meaning stage.

clue.text: One vegetable among many known by expert

definitions.meaning: a single bulb from a common kitchen vegetable sold by the string or sack
from the idiom 'know your ...', meaning to be expert in a subject

explanation.surface: A single vegetable out of a crowd that only a connoisseur would recognise.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition leans on the British idiom 'to know one's onions', meaning to know one's subject thoroughly.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of many kitchen bulbs, and the idiom says an expert knows their onions.

clue.text: Stuff poor homeless outcast initially into overcoat

indicators.note: the initials are put into the coat, so the word for the coat is split open to hold them

parts.note: an ulster is a long, loose, heavy overcoat, originally made in Northern Ireland

indicators.note: initially tells us to take the first letter of each of the three words before it

explanation.surface: Shoving a poor homeless outcast into a coat to keep warm.
explanation.walkthrough: An ulster is a long belted overcoat named after the Irish province; 'Stuff' is the verb, padding furniture, not the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To pad and cover furniture with stuffing and fabric is to fill it, a verb sense of stuff.

clue.text: Old Conservative joining British left in political alliance

explanation.surface: An elderly Tory throwing in his lot with the British left in a coalition.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are joined with British and left first, B and L, then O and C.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of nations or parties combined for a common political purpose.

clue.text: Desire middle-of-the-road position in New York area

parts.note: to long for something is to desire it
a traffic island is a raised refuge in the middle of a road

explanation.surface: Wanting a moderate stance somewhere in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle-of-the-road' looks like political moderation, but it is literal: a traffic island.
explanation.definitionFit: Long Island is the large island east of Manhattan, holding Brooklyn, Queens and suburbs of New York.

clue.text: Joint put right in the middle of top oven

indicators.note: the letter is put in the centre of the two-word run that follows, so that run is split to hold it

parts.note: the crown is the top of the head or of a hill
an oast is a kiln, an oven for drying hops

explanation.surface: Instructions to place a piece of meat on the top shelf of the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put right in the middle of' reads as cookery advice, but it sets R at the join of the two words. An oast is the hop-drying kiln of southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A crown roast is a joint of lamb or pork ribs tied into a ring like a crown.

clue.text: Irish writer's London college

definitions.meaning: belonging to Oliver Goldsmith, the Irish author of The Vicar of Wakefield
a college of the University of London in New Cross

explanation.surface: A London college named after an Irish author.
explanation.walkthrough: Goldsmiths is a college of the University of London, named after the City livery company, not the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive of Oliver Goldsmith's surname is also the name of a University of London college.

clue.text: Wreck a French affair

parts.note: un is the French for a
a do is an informal party or social affair

explanation.surface: A French love affair that ends in ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affair' suggests romance, but DO is a party.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo something is to ruin it or bring it to nothing, as wreck does.

clue.text: Genius hard to find among main college characters

indicators.note: the letter is put among the others, so the scrambled run is split to hold it
the letters, or characters, of the two words are taken and rearranged

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A brilliant figure is hard to find among the people at a leading college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' scrambles the letters to MICELANGELO; 'among' then slips H in after the C. 'college characters' pretends to be people at a college.
explanation.definitionFit: The Renaissance sculptor and painter is the byword for artistic brilliance.

clue.text: Dream experienced while doing boring job? That's a limited view

definitions.text: Dream experienced while doing boring job?
definitions.meaning: a vision seen by someone digging an underground passage, boring through rock
narrow focus on one aim, with everything else ignored

explanation.surface: A tedious day job breeds daydreams but a narrow outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like dull, but it means drilling through earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrow-minded fixation on one goal, excluding everything peripheral, is called this condition.

clue.text: Escort multitude into old jail

parts.note: to marshal people is to usher or escort them
a sea of faces is a multitude

explanation.surface: Guards herding a crowd into an old prison.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marshalsea was a London debtors' prison in Southwark, closed in 1842, known from Dickens's Little Dorrit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marshalsea was a prison in Southwark, south London, chiefly for debtors.

clue.text: Simple diet designed as discouragement from going on fast

indicators.note: designed means the letters are arranged into a new form

explanation.surface: A plain diet planned to stop someone starving themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going on fast' suggests dieting, but it means driving quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal maximum for road traffic deters motorists from driving too quickly.

clue.text: Dramatic effort that bears fruit

definitions.meaning: The ..., a 1929 political comedy by George Bernard Shaw
a barrow carrying a load of apples, literally bearing fruit

explanation.surface: A theatrical venture that pays off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bears fruit' looks like the idiom for succeeding; it is literal, a cart loaded with apples.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both Shaw's play title and a barrow carrying apples to market.

clue.text: Winner of pre-war beauty contest

parts.note: the Judgement of Paris, in Greek myth, chose the fairest of three goddesses before the Trojan War

explanation.definitionFit: Paris awarded the golden apple to the goddess of love, a judgement that led to the Trojan War.

clue.text: Greeting nobody outside house?

indicators.note: the nought stands outside, after the building rather than within it

parts.note: a hall is a large house, as in a country manor
O, nought, stands for nobody

explanation.surface: A hello called out when nobody is in the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts O at the end of HALL rather than around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hallo is a variant spelling of the word used to say hello.

clue.text: In promises, we ardently vow

indicators.note: In says the answer sits within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Making promises and fervently pledging oneself.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is in promiSES WE ARdently.
explanation.definitionFit: To vow is to promise solemnly, as an oath does.

clue.text: Expression of sympathy for actor's difficulty?

definitions.meaning: a dated British phrase meaning bad luck
a part with tough speeches to learn: difficult words in a script

explanation.surface: Commiserating with a performer who is struggling.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a British idiom like 'tough luck'; the second reads the words literally, as difficult lines in a script.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom offers commiseration, and literally it means tough speeches for a performer to learn.

clue.text: Soldier, for example, must follow every message — that's vital

indicators.note: the soldier comes after the other pieces, at the end of the answer

parts.note: all means every one
the import of something is its meaning or message
a soldier is a caste of ant

explanation.surface: An army man must obey every order, as it is crucial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldier' looks military, but a soldier is a type of ant.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of the utmost importance is crucial, the same sense as vital.

clue.text: Identify American that has banks in European countries

definitions.text: that has banks in European countries

parts.note: to tag something is to label or identify it

explanation.surface: Picking out an American bank that operates across Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' suggests finance, but they are river banks: the Tagus flows through Spain and Portugal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tagus is the Iberian river flowing through Spain and Portugal, so its banks lie in both countries.

clue.text: Upward drift to correct

indicators.note: in a down entry, upward means the word is read from the bottom up, backwards

parts.note: the tide is the drift or general flow of things

explanation.surface: A general shift upwards needs amending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upward' turns TIDE round in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text is to revise it, putting errors right.

clue.text: Make harsh pronouncements in place of vicar

definitions.meaning: to speak loudly and harshly, like a donkey
the parish of the Vicar of ..., the turncoat cleric of the English song

explanation.surface: A vicar delivering harsh words from his pulpit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vicar of Bray, in the 18th-century English song, changed his creed to keep his living under each monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey's harsh noise is a bray, and Bray is the Berkshire village of the song's vicar.

clue.text: Wrestling ring figure entered initially

indicators.note: the figure is entered first, so it comes at the start, before the ring

parts.note: a sum is a figure, a total
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A wrestling ring with a number entered on it first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entered initially' puts SUM first, before O.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumo is the Japanese style of wrestling between heavyweights in a ring.

clue.text: Academic with endless fire within is main troublemaker

indicators.note: the fire is put within the academic, so that word is split to hold it

parts.note: a reader is a senior university lecturer in Britain

indicators.note: endless means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: an ingle is a fire on a hearth, as in inglenook

explanation.surface: A scholar with burning zeal who leads the trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' drops the final E of the fire; 'within' sets the rest after the first letter of the academic. A reader ranks just below a professor at British universities.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringleader is the chief instigator of a group causing mischief.

clue.text: In test, this wine is best liked

indicators.note: the clue says this word goes in another word to make a third, so we take that word back out

parts.note: tastiest means most appetising, the best liked

explanation.surface: In a tasting, this wine is the favourite.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'put this wine in test and you get best liked': the wine slipped between the first T and EST makes the word for best liked, so taking test away leaves it.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is the sparkling white wine of Piedmont in north-west Italy.

clue.text: There's a point in spreading story when it's this

definitions.text: There's a point in spreading story when it's this

indicators.note: the point is put in the scrambled letters, so they are split to hold it
spreading means the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: W, west, is a compass point

explanation.surface: Some stories are worth broadcasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spreading' scrambles the story letters to NEWSORTHY; 'in' slips W after the S. The whole clue also defines it: there's a point in spreading a story worth reporting.
explanation.definitionFit: A report worth publishing is one with enough interest to merit being spread as news.
